title: Ministers
lead: India's Council of Ministers is the ==‘efficient secret’== of the Constitution — the real power dressed in constitutional language that locates authority in the President. ==Read with MCN 33.==

head: Amendment
Key change
rows: President ==bound by ministerial advice== — discretion removed.
President may return advice ==once== for reconsideration; must then act.
Tenth Schedule — affects ministerial appointments from defecting legislators.
Cap on the Council of Ministers — ==max 15% of Lok Sabha strength==.

items.title: Cabinet Ministers
bullets: Highest rank — attend all Cabinet meetings with ==full voting rights==
Head major departments: Finance, Home, Defence, External Affairs
Usually ==20–25== in practice

items.title: Ministers of State
bullets: ==Independent Charge==: heads a ministry; functions almost like a Cabinet Minister but ==doesn't attend Cabinet== unless invited
==Without Independent Charge==: assists a Cabinet Minister

items.title: Deputy Ministers
bullets: Third tier — assist a Cabinet Minister or MoS; ==don't attend Cabinet==
Rarely appointed since the 1970s–80s; ==not in current Union practice==

items.title: Parliamentary Secretaries
bullets: ==Not constitutionally mentioned==, but used in States (Delhi, TN, HP)
[[Bimolangshu Roy v. State of Assam (2017)]]: struck down as violating ==Art 164(1A)== — enlarging the ministry beyond the cap

blocks.text: The UPA used GoMs and EGoMs extensively — ==over 25 active GoMs by 2013==. Critics argued this ==paralysed decision-making and diffused accountability== (a minister could always blame the GoM). Most were abolished after 2014.

sections.title: Impact of the Cabinet System on Parliamentary Democracy

items.title: Strengths
bullets: ==Fusion of powers = responsive government== — executive-legislative alignment ensures stable policy passage
==Accountability mechanisms work== because ministers are also parliamentarians — Question Hour, Zero Hour, no-confidence
==Collective decision-making== — no single person can unilaterally commit the state (in theory)

items.title: Harms
bullets: ==Whip + anti-defection = legislator as rubber stamp== — a backbencher cannot effectively criticise without risking disqualification
==Coalition compulsions → policy paralysis== (UPA 2, 2010–14); ==no-action as policy==
==Question Hour dysfunction== — ~70 sitting days/year vs 120+ in the Nehru era; point-scoring over substance
==Delegated legislation hollows out Parliament== — COVID lockdown, demonetisation, Art 370 executed with minimal Parliament time

==The fusion that corrupts== — government dominance of the Business Advisory Committee; bills passed without Standing Committee scrutiny. ==Cabinet should be accountable TO Parliament, but controls it instead==

items: ==Ministerial Code==: UK has a detailed, PM-revised Code on ethics, conflict of interest, civil-service relations. ==India has no equivalent== — the Transaction of Business Rules cover procedure, not ethics.

==Parliamentary questions==: UK has ==PMQs every Wednesday==, live and televised, answered by the PM personally. India has no equivalent — the PM is rarely present in Question Hour; ~20 starred oral answers a day.
==Individual responsibility==: UK strong — ==Dominic Raab (2023)== resigned after a bullying inquiry. India weak — no resignation over the 1984 riots or the COVID-19 oxygen shortage.

==Civil service==: UK has a permanent, politically neutral service with clear separation of political direction and execution. In India transfers, postings and deputation are ==heavily politicised== — and ‘Babu Raj’ can see senior IAS officials capture new, non-expert ministers.

sections.title: Who Should Be a Minister — Criteria & Size

head: Ideal criterion
Rationale
rows: Essential for the ==climate–health–water nexus== type of challenge

items: ==Legal criteria (Arts 75, 164)==: eligible to be an MP; citizen; ==25+ (LS) or 30+ (RS)==. The Constitution mandates ==no educational qualification, no prior experience, no clean record== unless conviction disqualifies. In [[PUCL v. UoI]] the SC observed PM/CMs should uphold constitutional morality and avoid persons with ==serious criminal antecedents==.

==Political criteria==: parliamentary strength and loyalty; ==coalition accommodation== (Railways, Petroleum, Telecom to key allies); regional balance; ==caste/community/gender representation==; domain expertise (technocrats, ex-civil servants, economists, diplomats); public communication ability.

items.title: Supporting the 15% Cap
bullets: ==Checks patronage politics==
Enhances Cabinet ==efficiency and coherence==
Compels prioritising ==competence==

items.title: Against the Cap
bullets: ==Still allows 70–80 ministers== — overlap and diffusion
==Too many MoS without real power== → ‘who is actually responsible?’

items.title: May Become Too Low
bullets: ==Governance is more complex== — AI regulation, renewables, semiconductors, cybersecurity, blue economy
==Super-ministries== (Finance, Home, Health, Climate) need capable junior ministers

items.title: Criminalisation
bullets: ==ADR 2024: 251 of 543 LS MPs (46%)== declared criminal cases
Several Modi 3.0 ministers had declared cases at oath-taking
==‘Mafia-to-minister’ pipeline== — Atiq Ahmed (UP), D.P. Yadav

items.title: Oversized Cabinets (Pre-91st CA)
bullets: No cap before 2003 — expansion for caste, regional, coalition compulsions
==Deve Gowda (1996)==: 33 Cabinet Ministers + numerous MoS
Indira Gandhi's cabinets at times ==exceeded 60 members==

items.title: Conflict of Interest
bullets: Portfolios in sectors of personal business interest
==No dedicated conflict-of-interest legislation== (unlike Australia, Canada, UK)
Mining insiders as Mines Ministers; developers as Housing Ministers

items.title: Lack of Expertise
bullets: ==No constitutional requirement of subject expertise==
Health without medical/public-health background; Finance without economists
Contrast: ==France, Germany, Scandinavia== appoint technocrats

items.title: Bureaucratic Capture
bullets: Dependence on senior IAS/IFS officers → ==‘file raj’==
Or the reverse: ==politicisation of the bureaucracy== through loyalty-based postings

items.title: Sinecures & Corruption
bullets: Post-retirement Governorships, Commission chairs, ambassadorships — a ==‘revolving door’== undermining NHRC, UGC etc.
==2G Spectrum, CWG, Coal Scam, Fodder Scam, Saradha==

items.title: Codes & Conflict of Interest
bullets: Enact a ==Ministerial Code== — conflict of interest, use of resources, civil-service relations, standards of conduct
Models: ==UK Ministerial Code==, ==Canada's Conflict of Interest Act (2006)==, Australia's Statement of Ministerial Standards
The ==2nd ARC== recommended a comprehensive code of ethics — ==yet to be implemented==
Publish a ==Cabinet Manual== (UK 2011, revised 2022)

items.title: Oversight & Capacity
bullets: ==Mandatory Standing Committee referral== of all bills (Venkatachalaiah Commission)
A ==PMQs-equivalent== weekly ‘PM's Parliament Time’
==Fixed calendar: at least 100 sitting days/year== (currently ~65)
==Senior Minister–Technical Adviser pairings== with shared accountability (Germany, Singapore models)
==‘Ministerial Accountability Act’== defining resignation triggers; committees empowered to ==censure individual ministers== (New Zealand model)
==Fixed tenure and Civil Services Board== per [[T.S.R. Subramanian v. UoI (2013)]]
==Sunset GoMs== — automatic dissolution if no report in 6 months

blocks.text: Every unaccountable minister, every bloated cabinet, every conflict of interest unaddressed is a democratic debt left unpaid. India's parliamentary democracy does not need a new constitution. It needs ministers worthy of the one it has.

Collective responsibility is the ==constitutional glue== that holds the executive together — transforming a group of ministers with diverse views into a unified political entity that must ==rise and fall together== before the people's representatives.

head: Case
Holding
rows: Ministers must ==defend Cabinet decisions inside and outside Parliament==, regardless of personal opinion.
Every minister is responsible for every decision, agreed or not — but a minister's ==personal remarks don't bind the government==. Accountability flows ==from Cabinet to minister==, not the reverse.
Two dimensions: ==unified policy support==, and ==shared success or failure== of policies.

blocks.text: ==Dr B.R. Ambedkar resigned in 1953== over the Hindu Code Bill — the expected ethical consequence of dissent: ==resignation, not public opposition from within office==.

head: Aspect
Regular Cabinet
Shadow Cabinet (UK)
rows: Shadow Ministers for the same portfolios

items: ==Individual vs collective==: Art 75(3) mandates collective responsibility; individual responsibility is a ==weaker convention in India==. UK — ==Crichel Down Affair (1954)==: Minister Dugdale resigned over administrative failure with no personal involvement. India — 2G (A. Raja), CWG, Coal scam saw ==no preemptive resignations==.

head: Effect
India
Comparative
rows: Jaitley publicly defended demonetisation (2019) despite internal reservations
==Robin Cook resigned (2003)== over Iraq rather than criticise from office
Maneka Gandhi had to align environmental/animal-welfare norms with economic priorities
Boris Johnson as Foreign Secretary constrained on a harder Brexit line
GST rollout (2016) — Finance, Commerce, Consumer Affairs compromised for a unified stance
UK coalition (2010–15): Lib Dem ministers compromised on austerity
==Arif Mohammad Khan resigned (1986)== over the Shah Bano dilution
Manmohan Singh privately persuaded sceptical ministers on 1991 liberalisation
==Shashi Tharoor's dismissal (2010)== after the IPL controversy
Thatcher's reshuffles removing open dissenters (Geoffrey Howe)
Vajpayee coalition — Jaswant Singh and Yashwant Sinha coordinating jointly
New Zealand Cabinet Manual explicitly frames ==‘team government’==
COVID health/migrant criticism ==couldn't be pinned on one minister==
Uniform welfare messaging (Jan Dhan, Ujjwala, Swachh Bharat) reduced portfolio experimentation
Canada: consistency in bilingual policy across ministries

head: Aspect
India
United Kingdom
France
United States
rows: Strong convention — Cabinet must retain Commons' confidence
To the National Assembly, but also influenced by the President — ==dual accountability==
==None to the legislature== — Cabinet not drawn from it
Ministers responsible for their departments; removable by PM
==Strong tradition== — resignations for departmental failure (Profumo Affair)
Exists but diffused by President–PM duality
Weak — Secretaries rarely resign absent congressional pressure
Criminally/civilly liable; prerogative reviewable (GCHQ, M v Home Office)
Prosecutable; ==Conseil d'État== handles most legality matters
Very strong — Question Time, Select Committees, confidence votes
Conditional — falls only on a ==Motion of Censure==
Weak — hearings but no dismissal power
PM advises President; no-confidence collapses the Council
Cabinet resigns on losing the Commons
Assembly vote OR ==President dissolves the Assembly==

items: ==Constitutional head of government== — ‘head of the Council of Ministers’ (Art 74); the ==real executive== behind Art 77
==Leader of the Lok Sabha majority== — controls confidence, Money Bills, legislative agenda, guillotine
==Chair of the Cabinet== — decides size, portfolios, agenda, GoMs, crisis architecture
==Nodal point between party and state== — enforces discipline through the whip and Tenth Schedule
==National security, foreign policy, finance core== — PMO deeply involved in Defence, Home, Finance, MEA, Atomic Energy, Space

==‘First among equals’ — but only sometimes==: high Cabinet government (early Nehru) → ==PMO centralisation== (Indira post-1969) → ==coalition constraint== (1996–2004) → ==re-centralisation== under stable majorities

blocks.text: The Prime Minister is the pivot of the parliamentary system, combining political authority with administrative leadership. The office thrives when it leads collaboratively and governs constitutionally.

items: If a Minister (==including the PM==) is arrested and detained for ==30 consecutive days== on allegation of an offence punishable with ==5 years or more==, the President (on PM's advice) must remove the Minister.
For a CM/State Minister, the Governor acts on CM's advice; if the CM is themselves in custody 30 days, they must resign.
If removal doesn't happen by the ==31st day==, office ==ceases automatically==.
==Re-appointment allowed== once released. ‘Serious offences’ = ≥5 years' imprisonment under any law in force.
==Status: still a Bill==, not enacted — provisions are prospective.

items.title: Impacts on Appointments & Governance
bullets: ==Greater risk for ministers with serious charges== — parties may screen more carefully
==Pressure on PM/CMs to act quickly== — reduces discretion; more legally-triggered removals
==Room for political-legal manipulation== — trigger is detention, ==not conviction==
Coalition negotiations may insist on ==clean-profile ministries==
New ==structural risk to government stability== (coalition fallout, regional imbalance)
Symbolic ==integrity narrative== — ‘no minister should run the government from jail’

items.title: Critiques & Constitutional Issues
bullets: ==Presumption of innocence== — removal on detention, not conviction
==Separation of powers / misuse risk== — prosecution machinery can trigger political removal
==Ambiguity==: which law? how is detention defined? bail within 30 days as a safe harbour
==Automatic cessation vs political accountability== — shifts removal from legislature to a quasi-legal trigger, impacting ==collective responsibility==
Risk of ==sidelining political opponents== via arrest

blocks.text: In a democracy, the demand for integrity in public life is non-negotiable. But integrity must be secured through law, not at the cost of justice. The 130th Amendment's real test lies not in its text, but in how responsibly the State wields it.
